scenes.heading: Context Cancellation & Timeouts
scenes.narration: Let's take a minute on context.Context, Go's mechanism for carrying a cancellation signal and a deadline across goroutines.

scenes.heading: The core idea
items: ctx.Done() closes on cancel, timeout, or a parent cancel
Goroutines select on it to stop work immediately
Cancellation is cooperative — code must observe it
scenes.narration: A context carries a cancellation signal and an optional deadline. When you cancel it, manually, on a timeout, or because a parent was cancelled, its Done channel closes. Every goroutine selecting on that channel wakes up and can stop immediately. The crucial subtlety is that cancellation is cooperative: it only closes Done. A goroutine that never checks the context keeps running, so you must write code that observes it.

scenes.heading: Lifecycle of a WithTimeout context
steps: Derive with WithTimeout; a runtime timer arms
Pass ctx as the first arg down the call chain
Work finishes, or the timer fires first
defer cancel() releases the timer immediately
scenes.narration: Deriving a context with WithTimeout creates a child and arms a runtime timer. You pass that context as the first argument to every operation, and each selects on Done at its blocking points. Then it's a race: either the work completes, or the timer fires. Whichever happens, Done closes and ctx.Err reports why, either DeadlineExceeded or Canceled. Finally, defer cancel releases the timer and unregisters the child right away.

scenes.heading: Race work against a deadline
scenes.narration: This races a slow operation against the context. Notice the result channel is buffered with capacity one. On timeout, the select takes the Done branch and fetch returns, but the worker goroutine is still sleeping. Because the channel is buffered, its later send succeeds into the buffer and the goroutine exits cleanly. An unbuffered channel here would leak one goroutine on every timeout.

scenes.text: Always defer cancel(); pass ctx as the first argument, never store it; in CPU loops poll ctx.Err() periodically.
scenes.narration: The rules to live by: always defer the cancel function to release timers, even on the timeout path; go vet flags a missed cancel as a leak. Pass context as the first argument and never store it in a struct. And since cancellation is cooperative, tight CPU loops should poll ctx.Err every few thousand iterations to stay responsive without measurable overhead.
